speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question of privilege arises out of debate concerning Bill C-93.
During report stage debate, the government introduced some new figures. The debate very much hinged on the efficiency and cost savings to be achieved by bringing the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council and the external cultural program into the Canada Council.
We heard testimony from Treasury Board, the Privy Council as well as Finance in committee stating there were no savings. We tried as well to bring in the minister and the people from the Canada Council in order to allow us to verify whether there would be any savings and efficiencies. We were not allowed to do that. During the debate the government introduced a new set of figures, claiming some $5 million per year in savings will be achieved.
It is important as a member of Parliament that I know where these figures come from and that I have an opportunity to review them because they are important in determining what position we will take on this bill. It is also important to the academic community because, as would members on this side of the House, it would like to see greater efficiencies and cost savings. We would like to see that this is proven.
I believe my grounds for the question of privilege are that my ability to perform my duties as a member of Parliament have been infringed. As well, the authority and the dignity of Parliament and of all members have been offended by the action of the government. The action in question is the introduction of new and previously unavailable and arguably withheld evidence to the House. The lack of the evidence in question affects my judgment as a member and potentially the judgment of my party. In short I have a right to examine the evidence and to draw conclusions, a right I tried to exercise in the committee without success.

Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to begin the debate at third reading of Bill C-93.
We on this side of the House have worked relentlessly to reduce the size and cost of the federal government. We have restrained federal spending, including public sector wages. We have implemented the Spending Control Act and the debt servicing and reduction account to ensure that fiscal responsibility is a matter of law. By privatizing over 20 Crown corporations we have reduced the public payroll by 50,000 employees. Nevertheless, we
April 23, 1993

realize, as do Canadians, that the task of streamlining the federal government and making it more efficient is not yet complete. Bill C-93 is a further step in that direction.
Bill C-93, the budget implementation bill, is the second of a series of omnibus bills designed to give effect to the government streamlining measures announced in the 1992 budget. The first one, Bill C-76, received royal assent on April 2, 1993 and a third one, Bill C-92, dealing with the Income Tax Act and other technical measures is proceeding to second reading in the other place.
The purpose of the Bill C-93 is to reduce government overhead and to provide services to Canadians more efficiently. The Bill includes the necessary amendments required to give full effect to the budget decisions affecting 14 organizations.
Contrary to the campaign which my friends opposite have waged with their filibuster of this bill in the House and with their allies through the media, this bill is not simply a "cuts" exercise, and its success will not be measured only in the calculation of dollars and cents over the short term.
As we are bound to repeat once again for the benefit of the opposition, there will be savings over the longer term as the size of government is reduced and overhead costs are diminished, and this is precisely what Canadian taxpayers wish to see.
More to the point, these changes are part of our broader commitment to smaller, simpler, more cost-effective government, able to provide Canadians with the programs and services they need in the challenging circumstances of the 1990s and at an acceptable cost of delivering them.
I want now to review some of the more contentious issues raised in earlier debate with respect to specific organizations addressed in Bill C-93.
The positive features of Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation or ECBC will be retained after the Corporation is merged with the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, commonly called ACOA. In particular, financial assistance will continue to be available for new and existing businesses that are likely to make a substantial contribution to industrial development and employment opportunities in Cape Breton Island outside of the coal
Government Orders
producing and steel industries. ACOS's new statutory powers will be restricted to Cape Breton Island and a portion of mainland Nova Scotia around the town of Mulgrave.
Dissolving the ECBC and carrying over its specific statutory powers to ACOA will eliminate a duplication in program delivery and the administrative overlap which that duplication entails. ACOA clients in Cape Breton will be the beneficiaries of increased efficiency in promotion, financial assistance and development of industry on the island.
During debate on this part of the bill on Tbesday, April 20, 1993, the member for Regina-Qu'Appelle made reference to estimates of the costs and savings to government from the merger of ECBC with ACOA. I refer to page 18151 of Hansard. Specifically he stated that the merger would cost the government $1 million over five years.
The $1 million cost figure referred to by the member for Regina-Qu'Appelle was an early estimate of costs which was made prior to the February 1992 Budget and prior to any specific knowledge of the parameters of the integration of ECBC into ACOA. That estimate assumed far greater job losses and severance costs than will actually be the case, since most of ECBC's employees will be transferred to ACOA.
It is now estimated that there will be no additional costs to government as a result of the merger. The corporation, like any responsible corporation, has set aside annual contributions for employee termination benefits. There are sufficient resources in this fund to pay all anticipated severance costs associated with the merger.
With respect to savings it is estimated that the annual savings to government from merging ECBC with ACOA will be at a minimum $250,000. Saving could reach up to $1 million annually on the successful divestiture of ECBC'S industrial park and farm operations.

Next I want to deal with what appears to be the most difficult aspect of the bill for my friends opposite to get their minds around, Part III-the integration of the Canada Council with the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council and the international relations programs.
In spite of efforts by members on this side of the House to set the record straight, the opposition speakers continue to characterize this section of the bill as an empty exercise motivated by fears of the government having to cave into right wing political pressure.
They are, of course, entitled to their opinions, but I am here again today to tell the House that this government will not be put off from finding reasonable and prudent ways to relieve the burden on the Canadian taxpayer whether the pressure is coming from the so-called right or from any other self-serving lobby.
This merger, once the transition has been completed, will result in increased efficiency in the delivery of programs and services. I am talking about grants to artists, promotion of the arts and the provision of scholarships in the social sciences and humanities and enhancing our capacity to project our national personality and the expression of our culture abroad.
The opposition continues to demand of us why are we proceeding with this merger. The answer remains straightforward and has not changed since they first posed the question at second reading: to improve program delivery and reduce overhead. Let me say one last word about the operation of the councils. It is important to recall, as my colleague from Winnipeg South told the House on Wednesday, the Canada Council worked well as one council for over 20 years.
Over time, the council developed a structure adapted to the two clienteles with the creation of an Academic Advisory Panel as a parallel to the Advisory Arts Panel, and the establishment of a separate administrative staff to deal with the academic community.
The differentiation of roles between the two was fully understood and accepted by the two bodies and their relationship was characterized by mutual respect.
It is also significant to note that in its appointments to the new council, the government of the day took the Canada Council as its model and gave the new body, the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council, a predominantly lay composition and similar budgetary and expenditure practices.
The merger of the two councils in no way represents a lesser commitment to the academic community. The government is on record as saying that the interests of all its clients will be protected. Social research will in no way be compromised, as opposition members tried to say.

Madam Speaker, I hope this confirmation by Mrs. Paule Leduc will dispel the doubts that the opposition is trying to cast on the savings this merger will bring.
As we said on Wednesday, it is normal that in the first few years of operation there are costs associated with the merger. Nevertheless, we expect, based on the preliminary judgement which the management of both councils has given us, that reduction in overhead will result from a streamlined program structure with three-year funding instead of annual grants, simpler and more flexible financial management, co-location under one roof, rationalized common services-by that I mean personnel, financial and information-and the return to one governing body, one council, instead of two.
I congratulate my friends opposite for the entertainment they have provided the House and the public with their misleading attacks on this merger. We have been patient and have tried to correct the record a number of times. Now-enough is enough. There are significant ongoing annual savings asssociated with the merger in part III of Bill C-93 over the long term.
We have told the members opposite the magnitude of those savings and when we expect to begin to realize them. That should be sufficient. I know it is more than sufficient for the taxpayers of Canada.
I have one final point on the specifics of the recent debate on this bill. I am referring to the point raised by the honourable member for Regina-Qu'Appelle on part VIII of the bill and the debate on Motion No. 67 on Wednesday.
Although, this is a highly technical area of intellectual property litigation, I think that in his remarks on cost recovery, the member has confused user fees, passthrough costs and awarding of costs for frivolous proceedings. That would appear to be the case with his statements in Hansard on pages 18260 and 18261.
He argued that SOCAN will have to absorb the cost of frivolous proceedings brought against them. This is not the case. I refer the honourable member to page 80 of the Bill. Section 12 of the new Intellectual Property Tribunal Act clearly provides the Tribunal with the discretionary power to award costs against nuisance proceedings of this sort.
Therefore, I believe that SOCAN's fears in this regard are unfounded.
Moreover, Madam Speaker, you will allow me to point something out with reference to a remark the hon. member for Regina-Qu'Appelle made about me as recorded in Hansard of April 21, 1993, page 18260 and I quote:
Mr. Speaker, I really tried to follow what the parliamentary secretary was saying but I am afraid I am going to have to wait until I read Hansard tomorrow. I think what the parliamentary secretary was doing was just reading out what bureaucrats had told him to read out.

The thing is very simple. The government has a user pay policy. Take passports, for example. There was a time when even passports were subsidized, that is to say that the fees charged to the user were less than the production costs. Then the government came up with a policy to apply the user fee principle. The same principle applies to the Intellectual Property Tribunal.
And in that instance, we are only saying that SOCAN and other users will have to bear the operating costs of the Intellectual Property Tribunal.
Second, this particular amendment which would have added the word "user" or "consumer" could have been interpreted in such a way as to impose a tremendous administrative burden on the Intellectual Property Tribunal which, by law, would have had to take upon itself the tremendous burden of billing for its services.
I believe that SOCAN, which represents around
35,000	members, should bear the costs connected with using the Intellectual Property Tribunal and then charge its members. That way, the Intellectual Property Tribunal does not have to be laden with such a burden.

I also think it is important to remember that there are seven other parts to this bill and that they have drawn very little attention during our proceedings. In fact, there are sections of the bill with which the opposition have expressed their support, like the winding up of the Veterans land administration and its integration into the Department of Veterans Affairs.
As I mentioned at the beginning of my remarks, Bill C-93 is in line with the government policy, with the economic statement and with the 1992 budget aimed at providing Canadians with better services for less, at streamlining administrative costs and in the end at alleviating the tax burden of the people.
Ever since 1984, every bill presented with that intent, namely to slash government spending, to reduce the machinery of government and therefore administrative costs, everyone of those bills was systematically opposed

On third reading, they opposed the sale of government shares in Telesat Canada proposed in Bill C-38. They did not support the privatization of Petro Canada, Bill C-84, second session. The Liberals voted against the act respecting the control of government expenditures which was meant to cap government spending, Bill C-56, third session. They opposed Bill C-26, third session, a legislation to improve the efficiency and accountability of the public service. This is not surprising. When a party like the Liberal Party is in power for so many years and when we see that over a period of 12 years the deficit grew from $1.8 billion in 1969-1970 to $38.5 billion in 1984-1985, with an accumulated debt of $200 billion, it is not surprising.

Madam Speaker, I think the House has always had some leeway with regard to arguments behind our government policies in every debate which takes place in the House. I have been here since the beginning of the week to debate this bill and I have listened to speeches from my colleague's friends as well as from other hon. members which were far from relevant to this debate. As far as I am concerned I think I have kept my remarks well within the scope of the debate on Bill C-93.
What I am trying to explain is the filibustering the liberal opposition has been doing on Bill C-93. What I am trying to show here is that every bill like Bill C-93 has systematically been opposed to by the New Democratic Party and the Liberal Party.
What I was trying to say before I was interrupted by my colleague was that it was not surprising to see constant opposition against bills which are aimed at reducing spending while, in 12 years, the Liberal government kept increasing expenditures at the rate of 14 per cent. I was referring to an example which is really rather interesting. In 1974-75, Mr. Jean Chretien stated on page 7138 of Hansard of July 2, 1975 the following: "We have decided that restraint is necessary. In order to exercise restraint we had to cut back on planned expenditures". That year, expenditures went up by 28 per cent.
Systematic opposition by the Liberals to Bill C-93 is part of a tradition that has lasted for more than 25 years, and I can understand that.
In conclusion, I want to state once more the importance, for the Canadian people, that governments do everything that is needed and take fair measures to reduce government spending, streamline administrative costs and increase the efficiency of services for the Canadian people.
As I said, a recent survey in Terrebonne clearly indicated that this is the way we should go. Throughout this country, Canadians who work 40 hours a week or more and strive to make ends meet tell us that the tax burden is unbearable. They are fed up with taxes and they are sick and tired because we do not make appropriate decisions to streamline our costs and expenses and save money whenever it is possible.
We should never forget that public funds do not come from another planet, or from the opposition members' pockets but from all Canadian taxpayers. I think there is a constant lack of good faith on the part of the opposition. If only the opposition had supported the government in its spending cuts, even once, if the Liberal and NDP opposition had only once made suggestions about spending cuts. Instead, for nine years now-you have been here all that time, Madam Speaker, you know what has been going on-all we have seen in this place is filibustering without any consideration for the Canadian taxpayers' ability to pay.
Bill C-93 is in keeping with the approach set out in the 1992 budget where we announced that 40 organizations would be eliminated as the services delivered by these organizations are already provided by the private sector and that others would be consolidated. Tliis Bill C-93 responds to the 1992 budget. It will rationalize the delivery of several services to Canadians, contribute to more efficient government and reduce the burden of government on Canadians. That is something that we all want in this House and that all Canadians want as well.
Therefore, I urge all members of this House, on either side, to pass this bill so that it can be sent quickly to the other place and that we can finally achieve these savings.

That is what this government has done. The hon. member referred to misleading attacks. It is the government which is being misleading and I can prove it. He quoted a letter from Paule Leduc, a very honest letter where she says it might be possible to save a few dollars in the not too distant future.

He did not admit that particular saving could have been achieved if the government had simply asked these organizations to reach a particular precise budgetary target. It is not as a result of what the government is doing. It is because these organizations will be forced to reach targets, and my hon. colleagues know that full well.
They know full well that this will go down in the annals of history and the annals of government as the silliest, the flimsiest, the most superficial bill that has probably ever come forward. It has been a botched job right from the very beginning. The government is trying to put some glitz to it, a bit of shine. There is no glitz; there is no shine. It is a deceptive and destructive bill. It is one that will haunt this government.
Let me make one point very clear. No one in government is opposed to streamlining if it is going to save money, if it is going to bring about increased efficiency and effectiveness. However there are no savings here. There is no increased effectiveness or efficiency. There are no studies to show it. When we questioned the witnesses from Treasury Board and the Privy Council, and I shall share the quotes shortly, they had nothing, no studies. They admitted they had nothing. They were honest men and women, and I appreciate their honesty. They might have chosen to do something else but they chose to tell the truth and by telling the truth they have exposed this government's project.
Government Orders
Just so that people are very aware of what is happening here, let us look at what is going on. The government has decided to streamline, initially it said to save money. Then when it was found out that was not true in reality, what did it do? It started to go for increased effectiveness and efficiency. When that did not come forth then it tried to pretend that we in the opposition were being unfair.
Let us remember that what the government is doing is in fact trying to kill organizations that in some cases were already dead. It is removing organizations that have been dormant for years. Worst of all, dynamic and vibrant organizations were taken out completely because the Economic Council of Canada could not stand the heat. The government could not take that kind of criticism. One of the worst decisions it made was the merger of the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada with the Canada Council.
Let us remember this bill is wide ranging. It talks about the Agricultural Products Board. It talks about the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. It talks about the Canada Council for the arts and for research, the social sciences and humanities. It talks about the independent review commission for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the Intellectual Property Tribunal. It also addresses the Canadian Commercial Corporation and Emergency Preparedness Canada. It talks about the International Trade and Procurement Tribunal, the Petroleum Monitoring Agency and the Veterans' Land Administration Act. It is a wide-ranging bill. The government has failed, absolutely and totally failed to make its case.
Because of its vastness and because it is complex the government has tried to suggest to Canadians that there were savings, that this was a good move and that this would be more effective. We know it is not true. We know what this bill is all about. It is about killing those agencies that are dead, removing and killing those that are dormant, and sapping the strength out of those that are vital and dynamic because they were a threat to government.
This bill is about trying to reach the Reform Party agenda. They are kissing cousins and I shall have more to say about that.

April 23, 1993

April 23, 1993

The only responses so far have been a few band-aids supplied here and there, leaving us now with wharfs that have deteriorated to the point where it will cost millions to restore them to safe operational conditions.

The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the Department of the Environment have committed $12 million over the next five fiscal years to assist the Canadian fur trade to adjust to changing market realities and respond to the advancement of the management and humane trapping of fur.

Madam Speaker, Rosser is a municipality and town west of Winnipeg which I represent and live in. It is celebrating its 100th anniversary this year.
This area of Manitoba with its rich farm land has become home to many pioneer families and immigrants, such as my parents and many others.
The historic development of Rosser is fascinating as well as intriguing. General Thomas Lafayette Rosser was a classmate at West Point with the famous General Armstrong Custer. They fought opposite one another in the U.S. civil war, yet later renewed their friendship. About seven years before General Rosser surveyed the CPR line from Winnipeg to Saskatchewan as chief engineer he was preparing to lead a volunteer force to rescue General Custer at the Little Big Horn, but he was too late.
April 23, 1993

I am sure all Canadians are grateful to this great, colourful American general for his contribution to the early development of Manitoba.
I also would like to congratulate Reeve Allan Bea-chell, his council, and many volunteers for making the 100th anniversary of Rosser a lasting and memorable success.

Madam Speaker, April 17 was an important day for Ottawa.
Last Saturday marked the return to Ottawa of professional baseball as the Ottawa Lynx took the field in the International Baseball League. The first pitch was the culmination of years of effort by Howard Darwin, a dedicated entrepreneur and sportsman whose leadership and commitment to his community have benefited the people of Ottawa for many years and in many ways.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister.
I would like to begin by quoting from the statutes of the defence department. At the very beginning it says that the minister is responsible for the management and direction of the Canadian Armed Forces and the development of policy on national defence.
Yet we have a minister who has known of four serious incidents and has never reported them, has taken no action whatsoever to clear up what her own chief of defence staff has said is a breakdown of loyalty and discipline, and has rejected all calls for better preparation, training or equipment for troops. She now states as part of the new politics of exclusion that it is better if she does not come to Parliament to answer questions.
I ask the Acting Prime Minister, how can Canadians have any confidence with the serious problems affecting our peacekeeping troops in Somalia that the conduct of the defence department will be dealt with when the minister believes she does not have to be accountable to the people of Canada and to Parliament?
Is it not time that this government appointed a new minister who recognizes the need to manage the department and be responsible to the people of Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member is distorting what the minister of defence said and is misleading the House and the Canadian public about the circumstances.
As the Judge Advocate General stated yesterday, the minister of defence under the National Defence Act has certain duties that are similar to those of a judge. What the minister of defence said in respect of these incidents, two for which the investigations are carrying on, is that they could possibly lead to court martial legal proceedings. In respect to those incidents which have been the subject of many questions in this House, she is very much circumscribed in terms of what she can relate to the House without prejudicing the individuals involved in order to ensure that justice prevails.
April 23, 1993

It is in that context she said it would be easier not to respond to those questions because of the possibility of causing harm to the judicial process and the questions of fair play, the charter of rights and all of those things which come into play in view of her responsibility. She will be in the House on Monday and Tuesday.
The rest of the department and its operation, the Canadian Armed Forces as has always been the case and particularly under this minister, is running very well.

Madam Speaker, when it comes to raising questions in the House, they are not questions about the specifics of a particular investigation. They are about the conduct of the minister, the department, the impact on our peacekeeping troops and whether under these circumstances they are able to do the job for which they are assigned. Surely, a minister who says that it is better not to be in the House is one who is in direct violation of her responsibilities to live up to that mandate.
This is what I want to ask the minister directly. We have another major problem. Our troops in Bosnia have been given a new mandate to protect civilians against potential attacks. Yet by all expert judgments they have neither the equipment nor the numbers to fulfil that mandate. That puts them at serious risk. It is a matter of grave concern to us all. There has been no report, no explanation and no accounting from the minister of defence to this House of Commons or to the Canadian people on that very grave and serious circumstance.
I want to ask the minister, when are we going to find out what new rules of engagement our troops in Bosnia have been given? Will they be given new equipment? Will there be other troops provided to help reinforce the new mission that they are given? Has support from the United Nations been obtained for this mission? Most important, where is the Minister of National Defence to answer these questions?

Because of the equipment.

speechtext:
No, he was talking about Somalia and in general the Canadian Armed Forces. I would ask him to provide the evidence that the Canadian Armed Forces is not the efficient, capable and the world's best peacekeeper we all believe it to be. He is saying something else. I wish he would provide proof before he makes that accusation.
With regard to Bosnia and Srebrenica, in particular, the Canadian military now in Srebrenica is there to enforce the ceasefire, to disarm the Bosnian Muslims and to provide humanitarian aid to the wounded and weak. It is performing that role admirably. Obviously if there is a full-scale attack by the Serbians or the Bosnians it will not be able to defend Srebrenica. However that is not its mandate from the UN.
In terms of other countries being invited, the objective is very simple. It would like to raise the stakes to put a situation where there is a multinational force there so that any attack on the city by the Serbs or the Muslims would be, in essence, an attack on the entire world. It raises the stakes and the cost of any such attack, therefore increasing the likelihood that it will not occur. If the Canadian forces are attacked, they are the most experienced peacekeepers in the world. They are aware and capable of protecting themselves.

Madam Speaker, I have a quick response to the minister when he asks about the concerns we raised. The concern was raised by the chief of defence staff himself. He said there was a breakdown in discipline and leadership of our troops in Somalia. It would seem to me that any government or any minister who had any interest at all in the welfare of those troops would be in a position to respond to that very serious concern raised by the chief of defence staff.

We are faced with a crisis of confidence on the role of Canadians in Somalia, with high risks for troops in Bosnia, and a Minister of National Defence who stays away from Parliament and fails to recognize the seriousness of these events for Canadians.

April 23, 1993
Oral Questions
I want to ask the Acting Prime Minister to take immediate steps to replace the Minister of Defence with someone who recognizes the responsibilities of her position and will report to the House on the very serious events involving Canadian peacekeepers.

It is the
government that is incompetent, not the militaiy. It's the minister of defence.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The reality is that our troops in Yugoslavia, by all accounts from everything I have heard, are performing admirably. Why does the government think it is good that the Minister of National Defence will not answer questions about the military mandate given to our forces in Bosnia? speechtext: Madam Speaker, of course the Minister of National Defence never said any such thing.

To extrapolate from that the suggestion that covers the entire gamut of DND operations is absurd. She said no such thing.
The hon. member also said in his preamble that the Minister of National Defence disagrees with the CDS about the fundamental operations and therefore-

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member makes absurd allegations and then demands that the Minister of National Defence come here to answer these absurd allegations. Make reasonable questions and perhaps you will get reasonable answers.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the minister opposite is trying to build a case and trying to shield the Minister of National Defence in that opposition members somehow are asking specific questions with regard to possible criminal
April 23, 1993

investigations as to who did or did not do what. We are not asking for that kind of information.
Why does the government think it is good that the Minister of National Defence is too busy to answer questions about her own personal role and about ministerial responsibility? speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there is no crisis of confidence in the Department of National Defence. However there is a crisis of confidence in the Liberal Party because of what the polls are saying. In respect of the particular details of the incidents that have been asked about in this House and so on, I have provided all of the information I possibly can without prejudicing the cases. I am sure hon. members, deep in their hearts, when they get past worrying about the polls, will recognize that it is most unreasonable to be pursuing these kinds of questions.

When our peacekeepers are on the front lines in Bosnia and Somalia there are legitimate concerns. Let me suggest that with the very serious events taking place now in Bosnia and Somalia, none of which would interfere with the investigation or the legal proceedings and all of which have to do with the duties and the responsibilities of the Minister of National Defence under the Defence Act and, above all, have to do with

our peacekeepers in the field, the minister should be here in the House to respond.
Will the government not agree that her primary duty is for the safety and reputation of Canadian peacekeepers and her first responsibility is to the people of Canada, to the House of Commons and to our peacekeepers and their families to answer questions about these matters?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member said there are serious problems in Bosnia in respect of our peacekeepers. There are serious problems in Somalia in terms of their ongoing role.
Other than those incidents which are being investigated and which we talked about earlier, what are these serious problems that are not being addressed? What is the crisis?
He then proves my point. Instead of asking about these particular serious concerns he claims are there, he turns around and asks a question designed to damage the reputation of the Minister of National Defence. I think that proves the allegation I made earlier.

The questions are these, and I would be very interested if the minister were prepared to give us some specific answers. Can the government assure Canadians that Canadian troops have not been put in a completely indefensible position and that the government has in fact been successful in getting other UN members to have their troops in that enclave to join in the defence of Srebrenica?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

Madam Speaker, the answer to the first question is no, the Canadian forces have not been asked or ordered to defend Srebrenica against a full-fledged attack by either side.

April 23, 1993

They are there attempting to maintain the cease-fire and providing humanitarian aid. As I indicated earlier, there have been discussions with the British and French officials. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has had discussions with the British and French to see if we could internationalize the forces in Srebrenica, thereby escalating the price that would be paid by any aggressor that attacked the town itself, making it an attack on the entire world.
It is quite clear that the 150 Canadian troops could not defend Srebrenica on their own. If they are attacked, as I indicated earlier, given the long experience of the Canadian Armed Forces they are capable of taking necessary action to protect their own welfare.

Madam Speaker, the answer seems to be different from that of the Secretary of State for External Affairs who was quoted as saying she was making every effort to try to get other countries there.
I would appreciate it if the minister could clarify that. While he is on this feet, it would be appreciated if he could tell the House that. He asked for some specific questions.
In December, when our forces went to Somalia, it was reported that no rules of engagement covering our forces in Somalia had been adopted by the Government of Canada, by cabinet. I would like to know if rules of engagement have subsequently been adopted by the cabinet and, if so, would the minister explain to the House precisely what they say in respect of dealing with unarmed Somali, three of whom have been reported killed by Canadian forces in Somalia?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the rules of engagement are rules of engagement that apply to all the forces in Somalia. Indeed to give out the details of the rules of engagement would risk compromising the operations in Somalia. It would be contrary to the agreement we have.
However, a broad outline of the rules of engagement could be provided to the hon. member. I will look into providing him with a briefing if he truly is interested in that.
In terms of the rules of engagement, as I indicated they are international rules of engagement. We have agreed to them along with all the other countries that are participating in this operation.

Madam Speaker, there are certain rules and regulations that are secret, but policy and the role of a minister are public policy and for public knowledge.
The Official Opposition has the highest respect for all peacekeepers around the world. We are asking serious questions and we demand serious answers. The minister should not be making light of our questions as he did previously.
A spokesperson for the Department of National Defence stated this morning that the 150 Canadian peacekeepers are too ill equipped and outnumbered to provide any defence of the town of Srebrenica. Two Canadian platoons sent from Tuzla to reinforce the Canadian troops were turned back by Serbian forces. France and Britain have ignored Canada's SOS for more troops.
What plans does the government have to ensure the safety of our peacekeeping troops and prevent a wholesale slaughter of the now defenceless Muslims?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I dispute absolutely the allegation or the accusation by the hon. member that we have treated lightly the serious questions. The serious questions we have treated seriously, but there have been a lot of less than serious questions answered which we have treated with the respect they deserve.
In terms of the 150 peacekeepers in Srebrenica, as I indicated earlier of course that is not a sufficient force to defend Srebrenica against an all-out attack by either side. I indicated that. That is not the intent. That is not the purpose. That is not why the Canadian forces are there. They are there to observe the cease-fire, to implement the cease-fire and to provide humanitarian aid. So far the cease-fire is holding.
I have told the hon. member that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has talked to her French and British counterparts about getting troops from those countries in there to internationalize the force. They have not said no. They have not responded to the request. To translate that into a firm no, as the hon.
April 23, 1993

member did, is a distortion and not helpful to the understanding of this serious situation.
If in fact the Canadian troops are attacked as a result of a breakdown in the cease-fire and so on, they are the most experienced troops in the world in terms of defending themselves and would take necessary action to defend themselves.
We are not expecting that. We are not hoping for that. The cease-fire is holding. We are endeavouring through diplomatic means and other means to make alterations so that the cease-fire will become permanent and we will be able to make that an internationally protected enclave.

My supplementary question is for the same minister, Madam Speaker. His answers are just confusing the mandate even more.
Yesterday the Acting Prime Minister rose in the House and declared unequivocally that the mandate of the Canadian UN peacekeeping forces in Srebrenica is simply to disengage both sides. "Our troops will protect themselves only and not the inhabitants of the town", he said.
Today we learned from the media, not from the minister of defence, that the UN has ordered Canadian troops to defend Srebrenica which goes far beyond the original mandate of using force only to defend humanitarian convoys, which he just said earlier in his response.
Will the minister clarify for Canadians what is the main goal of the Canadian troops in Srebrenica? Is it consistent with the original mandate given by the United Nations? Canadians have a right to know.

The troops are there, as I said yesterday, which is entirely consistent with what I said today, to implement the cease-fire which is holding. They are there to help in disarming the Muslim troops who have given up their arms. They are there to help provide humanitarian aid. They were never there and they have not been ordered to be there to protect Srebrenica against an all-out attack from either side.

What we are trying to do through diplomatic means and through co-operation of other countries in the UN is to make the thing stable on a more permanent basis.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate being given the opportunity to continue my address on Bill C-93. As I pointed out, it is a massive bill that attempts to give a very false impression. The government is trying to suggest that it is streamlining government. It is saying that it will save money and bring about increased efficiency and effectiveness. Of course this is blatantly false.
No government official has given any proof of that. What is worse, there have been no studies to show it. We have called upon them time and time again. We know full well it is an attempt to reach the Reform Party's agenda, the Conservatives' kissing cousins.
There are no savings. There is no proof that there are. There is no increased effectiveness or efficiency. There is no proof that there is. There are no studies, but now in a moment of panic all of a sudden we see new figures appearing. Obviously the big hand of someone has come down and said: You better buttress our case. That is your job. I am sorry for the government, but it is too late.
Treasury Board officials provided no proof. Mr. Speaker, you should have been there because you would have felt, as I did, that it was so sad to see these poor officials out there trying to defend the indefensible.

They were hung out to dry. Then they brought in the big shooters from the Privy Council and I thought perhaps we would get some answers then. To be perfectly frank and without being unkind in any way, the best I can say is that it was no better than the first set of proofs. It was probably worse. In some instances it will cost more money to the Government of Canada. That is part of the testimony that was made.
Who is opposed to this bill? The government likes to pretend that it is us on this side of the House, and that is true. However virtually everyone who has been involved in this is opposed to this bill. The government has absolutely dismally failed to produce any shred of evidence, but what is worse, it has failed to produce even one credible witness who would say this is a good idea. That is how bad the government's case is.

April 23, 1993
Government Orders
I think you would agree with me, Mr. Speaker, that when one has such a flimsy case one should withdraw, one should restudy, one should reconsider, one should consult and one should see what could be done.
This bill deals with a number of agencies but let me focus on just a couple of them. For example, Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation was an economic development tool in one of the regions of the country that needs this kind of assistance. It is a region where the unemployment rate is high and where the number of people who require social assistance is high. What does the government do? It merged it. For what reason? To give the impression that it is doing something significant.
Let us go to one of the more contentious parts, which is the merging of the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council with the Canada Council.

In fact, Bill C-93 calls for the merger of several agencies operating in a totally different way. As you know, Mr. Speaker, Canada is faced with numerous serious social problems such as family violence, environmental problems, constitutional uncertainty, native issues, new reproductive technologies, illiteracy, sexual abuse, to name a few. These problems cannot be solved without contribution from social sciences and humanities.
The Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council, created in 1977, was given the responsibility for the programs managed by the Social Sciences and Humanities Division of the Canada Council. It got that responsibility. The government is now trying to eliminate an efficient human sciences research framework. That is what it is doing. The government proposal to merge this agency with the Canada Council is a step back and will in no way help to improve the level of federal support for human sciences research. It is unfortunate because we already have serious problems. Funding is inadequate and the social sciences and humanities community was never consulted about that merger. There was no consultation at all. I urge government to postpone the decision to merge the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council and the Canada Council. It would be a courageous gesture on their part and I ask government members to consider it.
As you know Mr. Speaker, in 1978, the government decided to create the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council as an entirely separate agency from the Canada Council. Over the years, we saw them develop very different traditions. In the area of social sciences, scientists work mainly within universities. They have developed a research activity and project evaluation system based on the scientific tradition of peer review. That is very important and we should not let it disappear.

I understand that it is one group testifying against the other and talking about efficiency, savings and effectiveness. Let me use an analogy. It will be appreciated.
Say I have doctors telling me that this is what I have from a physical, emotional or what have you perspective and that this is the treatment that I need. Say, on the other hand, that there are well intentioned people telling me something diametrically opposed to this. That is the case here. I am going to go with the doctors. I am going to go with what they say and not with what the well intentioned people say.
The doctors on these issues have told me something about the merging of Enterprise Cape Breton with the Atlantic Opportunities Agency, the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council with the Canada Council, the program for Canadian Studies Abroad also with the Canada Council as well as the Agricultural Products Board with the the Ministry of Agriculture as well as the winding up of the Canadian Copyright Board and the transferral of the functions of the Registrar of Trademarks that are currently exercised by the Trade-Marks Opposition Board into a new tribunal to be called the Intellectual Property Tribunal. It is that the current government deserves to be slapped with a nasty malpractice suit. That is what it deserves.
These mergers make as must sense as merging the regressive Conservative Party with the NDP. That is as much sense as it makes.
April 23, 1993

Government Orders

In any case I think it is very clear that this merger was denounced by all concerned. All the organizations that know about the situation of social research in Canada, as well as my party and the party to my left, have asked that Part III, which is the part that provides for the merger of the Canada Council and SSHRC, be withdrawn or, at least amended significantly. Of course, the government carries on and turns a deaf ear to the unanimous appeals made by the academic, scientific and artistic communities.

The government has opted for one stop shopping in its hopes to save money. I wish it were so. It hopes to recoup the popularity of the Canadian people. Unfortunately for those involved in Canada as a whole, this type of one stop shopping may well result in confusion rather than efficiency. That is exactly what is going to happen. One knows that.
There is another reason why I do not like this bill when we talk of effectiveness. Let me say why I do not think that a whole lot of thinking has gone into this. For example, we have had no assurance that the peer review of the government will continue, which is a fundamental principle with respect to research. We have no assurance that the board that will eventually be struck will be representative of the significant people who understand the new mandate. To that effect, I put in an amendment and the government rejected it.

This bill is so full of holes that one could drive a Mack truck through it and one big Mack truck, I assure you.
With regard to the removal of the academic relations division and the Canadian studies program from External Affairs, one can say that this useless transfer will generate more expenditures, while reducing the effectiveness of the programs. Let me give you just one example. The Deparment of External Affairs uses the diplomatic bag to reach the numerous foreigners who are linked to programs under the responsibility of academic relations. By being transferred to the Canada Council, this division will no longer enjoy that privilege. This represents tens of thousands of dollars more in postage, for each program. Do you see the contradiction? It is an obvious contradiction.
The International Council for Canadian Studies is concerned about this section of the bill on four counts. First, there is no assurance that the program of Canadian studies abroad will be maintained at its current level. There is none whatsoever. Second, its integrity may not be preserved separately from domestic programs. That is a serious one as well. Third, the essential link between foreign policy and priorities and program policy and delivery will be jeopardized. Fourth, the program will be more costly and less effective.
The fusion or merger of SSHRC with the Canada Council risks, as a parade of witnesses before the committee clearly pointed out, negating the progress that has been made. Just take a look at what is happening.
The government created separate councils in 1978. They proved themselves to be fiscally lean and responsible and then the government throws them back together. Those people still have the gall to call themselves the Progressive Conservative Party.
In my opinion such a bill has proven once and for all that the party across the floor is indeed the regressive party of Canada. It has taken several ingredients that simply do not mix, put them together and thrown them against the wall hoping that they will stick.
In committee the following groups made up of responsible people opposed the bill: The Canadian Conference on the Arts, the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada, the Canadian Federation of the Humanities, the Social Science Federation of Canada and the Canadian Association of University Teachers as well as most university presidents.
That is an impressive list of witnesses. Not one single witness had anything positive to say about this merger.
It is also worth noting that no studies were forthcoming. I want to stress this; there were no studies. Can one imagine going after a change like this with no studies as to the financial savings? Treasury Board officials did point to a $1 million start up cost for one of those initiatives. Can one imagine that? This once again has insignificant savings over the long run. If there was a $1 million start up cost savings in the long run, then one could argue that-

Many in the academic community see a real danger that SSHRC will face the deep budget cuts that have affected the cultural community.
That is what they fear. This is a smoke-screen for exactly that.
Despite their strong opposition of Bill C-93, academic and cultural organizations have not behaved inflexibly in this dispute.

A number of amendments to Bill C-93 have been proposed, the most important of which would ensure that parliamentary allocations for academic research and international programs are kept separate from endowment funds to support the arts and culture, and that the new council is well and fully representative of the various communities served.

Nothing in the country could replace the Economic Council-
-or nothing to do with the agencies in question. The Ibries, circa February, 1992, were simply feeling antsy about the Reform Party, especially in western Canada. As a sop to this sentiment, the agencies were axed and Bill C-93 took form.
The basic problem with the bill-one pointed out by a parade of witnesses before a Commons committee-is that the Canada Council, SSHRC, and External Affairs' cultural policies have quite different missions. Lumping them together will make things harder for both the expanded Canada Council and for the groups that deal with it.
As I indicated before it makes as much sense as trying to merge the party that forms the government that calls

I have relayed what some notable Canadians and journalists have said. Let me give some excerpts from committee testimony. We had eminent people such as the assistant secretary of the Treasury Board. This sort of inflexibility, in our view, is disastrous. We favour a much more empirical, though no less vigorous, approach to the management of federal expenditures.

The amalgamation has taken place without any consultation". I could read more of this into the text but I think I have made my point. "Again we are not at all opposed to sensible, indeed vigorous, economies in the administration of the present councils. The country obviously faces an urgent financial problem, but we are convinced that the costs of this merger greatly outweigh the benefits" and the letter is signed by Robert Nadeau, president.
These are responsible men and women from some of the country's most prestigious organizations and this is what they had to say.
Everyone will be interested in this. There were government members who recognized they had no case. There are sensible government members; I have never said otherwise. They recognized that they had no case. Then they started talking to their political masters to see if there could not be some sort of compromise, some sort of understanding, some sort of meaningful solution.
We had proposed, as had the party to the left of me, that perhaps we could strike part III, just set it aside and study it again. Then if the facts proved that the government's agenda was correct we would go forward. Of course we had a lot of confidence that that was not so but the government did not want to take the risk. Some members wanted to take the risk. They talked to their political masters, but the political masters came down with their big hands and said no, no, no. It stopped at that. We had an opportunity to do what was right.
When I saw that the government would not be sensible, would not remove part III in spite of all of the evidence from the senior bureaucrats at Treasury Board, from Privy Council, the journalists, the various organizations, university presidents and all of those national organizations that are held in high esteem, I asked what it was that could be done. Could there still be something done?
I thought of amendments. Let us at least talk to the organizations and see what amendments might perhaps make a bad thing a little less bad. I moved amendments which would substantially improve the bill as well as address serious concerns expressed by the various communities involved.
For example, I proposed a name change which would much more adequately reflect the composition of the new council. Did the government even look at that? No. I also proposed that separate budgetary appropriation votes be held so that funds to be used for arts were designated as such, so that funding for the social sciences and humanities were used for that purpose and so that money to be used for the administration of the council was used for that purpose. Did the government look at that? No.
These are reasonable proposals: change the name to reflect the various realities; have separate votes to give some additional security to those who are being deeply shaken with these changes. Through amendments supported by the Social Science Federation and the Association of Universities and Colleges, I also proposed that board membership be representative and that board members have a certain degree of expertise in the areas in question. That is what I proposed.

I suggested changing the name to reflect the reality of what was happening, to ensure that these various organizations could be identified. I proposed that separate budgetary appropriation votes be held so that we could see exactly how much would be spent in each sector.
Mr. Speaker, it is important and I know that you understand and are sensitive to it. I also suggested ensuring that any appointees to a board of directors to represent the organization and help run it should come from the various sectors that were merged to be part of this new entity.
I also asked that the men and women chosen be people who know the field, in order to avoid partisanship and appointing one's chums, one's friends and family members and so on. I wanted to ensure that there would be men and women-and there are many here in Canada- who thoroughly understand these different sectors and can give them outstanding leadership, because that is what it will take and you realize that because, frankly, this is a creation that does not stand up.

The government even refused that.
I had difficulty in understanding why it would refuse rescinding part III. I had a great deal of difficulty particularly after I saw some colleagues who were willing to talk, but they wanted to save face. I do not think it was

a good enough reason in view of all of the evidence, but I thought surely they would look at some of those amendments.
I made those amendments with respect to the merger of the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council with the Canada Council, but I also made additional amendments with respect to the review. This bill was presented a long time ago as a result of budget decisions made by the government. People asked what was going on because there had been no consultation. We recognized immediately that key organizations such as the Economic Council of Canada were being removed. Everyone knows the government needs help in the area of the economy. When there are 1.5 million people unemployed, 2.7 million people receiving welfare, over 2 million people being fed by the food banks this year, a deficit that is over $30 billion and a debt that has almost tripled since 1984, the government needs expert advice, but no. It zaps those councils and those associations that could have been of great assistance to it.
We tried to rescind the most critical part. What happened? Nothing. We put forward reasonable amendments to try to fix it a bit, to make something terrible at least more or less palatable. What did government do? It was totally inflexible. Totally, totally inflexible.
Of course, the government comes to this House today suggesting that it is we, the opposition. Well, I am sorry. Yes it is we the opposition, but it is also all those organizations I mentioned and many others throughout the land who are saying that this is no good, that there are no savings, that this is a smoke-screen and there are

no increased efficiencies or effectiveness. This is a government agenda to try to get Canadians to rally to its cause.
With this kind of smoke-screen and with this kind of deceit and manipulation, it is not going to happen. It is not going to happen. The government has been unreasonable. It had plenty of opportunity to fix it. It had many opportunities and it has failed. It would not listen.

The government wants Canadians to trust it. Yes, one of the leadership contenders said that. "Trust me." Believe you me, Mr. Speaker, Canadians are not going to trust this government any more because of the decisions it makes.
Initially, the parliamentary secretary pointed out that Liberals have consistently opposed legislation which his government has put forth. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is really not with pleasure that I rise today on third reading of Bill C-93. In fact it saddens me.
Unfortunately what I suspect is being completed here today makes it a sad day. It is a sad day for research in this country. It is a sad day for the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada. It is a sad day for the external cultural programs of our country. As well it is a sad day for our parliamentary tradition and our parliamentary institution.
The area of the bill we are debating that concerns me most is part III. It brings together the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council, the cultural programs of

April 23, 1993
Government Orders
External Affairs, the old Canada Council and folds them all into a new agency.
It is sad because the motivation behind this-I will come back to that at length in a little while-is purely political and short term. The idea grew out of the minds of a few people in Finance. We understand there was no consultation with the appropriate departments or ministers. Certainly there was absolutely no consultation with the social scientists and the humanities nor with the arts community. It was a decision made solely by a few individuals in Finance.
As has been pointed out over and over again in discussions in this House, when we had officials from the government, the Privy Council, the Department of Finance and Treasury Board none of them were able to give us any justification for the statement that there would be cost savings. In fact we obtained through freedom of information the government's own estimate of what the savings would be. That document showed there would be zero savings in the next five years.
I tried in committee to get the head of the new Canada Council as well as the ministers in front of us but that was turned down by government members on the committee.
I kept asking why they were doing this. The only rationale was it might save us some money. When we pushed them to prove this to us they were not able to do it. It was finally admitted by somebody from Privy Council that it was doable.
How sad it is that public policy on something as important as this is being determined purely on the political notion that it somehow or other might appease the right wing and that the right wing might continue to support the Conservation Party. That is the only rationale which really makes sense.
The parliamentary secretary lambasted us earlier in his comments. He said we are making the accusation that the government's motivation is purely political in order to appease the right wing.
I am not making that charge. My party and the opposition has not made that charge. The person who said that was Conservative Senator Finlay MacDonald. He is quoted in The Globe and Mail dated February 27, 1993: "The whole exercise might be nothing more than a
symbolic act to protect the party's right flank from the attacks from the dreaded Reform Party, to cause sufficient pain and spill enough blood to impress the voters. If true this might be good politics in the short term but it is not good public policy in the long run". Despite the accusations of the parliamentary secretary it is a Conservative senator who has made this charge.
Why are we so upset with this? First of all a few people in Finance who I suspect have no notion or understanding or appreciation what the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council is all about made this unilateral decision.
It is important to the social scientists because in 1987, as a result of recommendations of the Lamontagne royal commission looking into science policies, the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council was separated from the Canada Council. It was done after much discussion and consultation. At that time it was considered a victory for the social sciences because the social sciences and the humanities were recognized as a legitimate form of scientific inquiry, that the social sciences was a science and not an art. This is important. It is important we recognize that the social sciences and the humanities are a legitimate form of scientific inquiry and how important they are in this day and age.
We all hear about how fast the world is changing, the globalization, the scientific and technological changes. All of our lives are thrown into this mad rush of constant change. Our societies and our cultures are in constant total change. The only thing constant is change; psychological change, economic change, cultural change, technological change.
As we try to live with this, as we near the end of this millennium, it is essential for us as human beings if we are going to survive to begin to get an understanding of these forces of change. We need to use the best methods and tools available to us as human beings, which are our scientific tools, in order to begin to get some understanding and some grasp of these tremendous forces that are creating such a horrendous change in our lives.
I remember a few years ago attending the habitat conference in Vancouver and listening to Buckminster Fuller. He stated that most of the major discoveries which have occurred in the history of the human race
April 23, 1993

occurred in his lifetime. I think that conference was in 1975.
What we see here today is the government, through its short-term political agenda, now moving the clock back. It is now stating that the social sciences are not really a proper scientific body and that they belong with the arts. We hear government members saying this. We heard the member from Winnipeg. I am sorry but I do not know her constituency. She said in the House the other day that the social sciences and the humanities were with the Canada Council for 20 years and what was good enough then is good enough now.
I am frightened when I hear such points being raised in the House of Commons of Canada. It is scary because one of the important tools, as I mentioned, in which we can begin to survive and get some control over the changes affecting our lives is through proper research, study and investigation of the social sciences. To again think of them as really being like the arts is a step back. It is a step that weakens one of the important tools we have as human beings.
What are some of the areas in which the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council are involved? It is involved in some of the research programs that deal with physical and monetary policy, urban development, productivity, economic and strategic planning, managing for global competitiveness, scientific and technological policy, family violence, the aging population, racism, sexism and youth unemployment. All of these are questions that concern social scientists. The type of debt we have is a question that concerns social scientists. It requires scientific study so we can begin to work our way out of the tremendous debt problem we have both at the federal and provincial levels. What the sciences attempt to do is minimize the human harm.

Mr. Speaker, I do want to speak on this very important bill, Bill C-93. I want to speak on it for some very fundamental reasons.
We have heard from many Canadians, whether they are in my constituency, across Canada or opposition members, as surprising as that may sound, that government has to find ways of controlling its expenses, it has to eliminate duplication, and it has to cut the levels of service. It must do so not so that there are fewer programs but that there is a more efficient way of delivering those items to the Canadian public. Bill C-93 is a direct result of some of those requests by Canadians.
The minister in the budget of a year ago, in February 1992, announced we were going to make a number of changes to the way in which the government delivered some of its programs through some of its agencies.
I am pleased that the government is doing that. I find it interesting in terms of the members of the opposition that come election time we will have one party talking about how it is going to reduce the deficit and the debt as part of the GNP but yet it will not identify how it is going to do it.
Today in Ontario the NDP have finally recognized that it cannot spend money like drunken sailors and it has to take some responsibility for its actions. It is going to wind up a few things, and that is most appropriate.
The difference between us here in Ottawa, the Government of Canada, and the Ontario NDP, the Government of Ontario, is that in Ontario it chose last year to spend the money and now it has to explain how it is not going to spend it, how it is going to withdraw some of the spending it did.
Well, here we are. We did not spend the money in last year's budget. We said that rather than spend it we are going to find ways of reducing our expenditures. These changes marginally affect the 1992 budget, but they have ongoing implications in years two, three, four and five as we get into the implementation of these changes.
April 23, 1993

Those kinds of savings, a dollar here, a dollar there, are very important to the over-all budget of Canada. I do not want to suggest that there are only dollars involved in these savings because there is substantially more than that.
It is important to understand the process from where we start because while we sit here and debate the issues that face Canada there are new issues that we face all the time. There are new problems that our constituents are demanding we face and that we find funds to deal with. That is always a challenge because the taxpayers at the same time argue we need new programs. They want these issues dealt with but they do not want us to spend any more money because they do not want us to raise taxes.
The Government of Canada implemented a bill called the Spending Control Act. That bill basically limited the amount of money the government can spend each year. That bill went out some four or five years into the future and said that each year we can increase by about 2.5 per cent or 3 per cent. That bill was put in place.
That bill said if we want to fund a new program, if we want to solve a new problem that has come along, if we want to spend some more money we are going to have to take that money from somewhere else in the system.
