subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION (GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATIONS) ACT, 1992 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to participate in third reading of Bill C-93 and being able to follow my learned and distinguished colleague from Ontario. He has made a number of observations on government restraint and government cutbacks as they relate to the deficit.
My colleague opposite comes to this Chamber with great sincerity and with perhaps a sense of false security about his future which is obvious to all those who understand the political nature of the country. We also know that repeatedly the hon. member for Ontario has shown himself to be a man who has focused himself and his political career, short lived that it will be, on the elimination of the deficit.
The hon. member in achieving his goal of deficit elimination has not been very successful because he and his colleague, particularly the President of the Treasury Board who happens to join with us today, have been inept. I am forced to use the word and regrettably so, but I am sure you will understand, Mr. Speaker. They have been incompetent in understanding the game or the practice of how to reinvigorate an economy which has been in recession for an extended period of time. I have listened and I have learned from members opposite that they do not possess the political will or the know-how to address the issue of deficit reduction.
Deficit reduction is directly related to economic growth. Without economic growth there will not be a reduction in the deficit. Somehow the President of the Treasury Board and the Minister of Agriculture who travel the world in various forms have not learned or do not understand that we must have a growing economy to reduce the deficit.
We have heard from minister after minister, leadership candidate after leadership candidate, that their only purpose in public life is to cut, cut, cut. If we were to follow the logic of the opponent of the President of the Treasury Board, the Minister of the Environment who says he will eliminate the deficit in four years, we would have to get rid of old age security. We would have to do away with medicare. We would have to do away with veterans affairs. Is that what they want in this country? I think the answer is no.

April 23, 1993
Government Orders
I am a little reluctant to say anything further on the remarks of the hon. member for Ontario who is not here at the moment, but he has made some outlandish statements with regard to controlling the deficit. He makes specific reference to Bill C-93. In his remarks he said: "Another board that will save lots of money is Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation".
I spoke on this matter at second reading as well as at report stage and I presented a number of amendments thereto which unfortunately were not accepted by members opposite. Nevertheless, I think it is worthwhile to note that that particular agency was earmarked to be a tool for economic development on the island of Cape Breton.
It is not I but the Tory senator who for all practical purposes is now running the campaign for one of the leadership hopefuls, the Minister of National Defence. The senator in question is Senator Lowell Murray of the other place. He is the gentleman who said not less than five years ago in the Hansard of the other place that Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation was a nation-building exercise. It was a nation-building measure, to be certain. That is what he said then. It was to foster economic development in an area of the country stricken with high unemployment. In fact, just the other day the statistics became available. It is 29.4 per cent, a shamefully high level of unemployment.
What is the government's response to that? It does away with the very corporation it put in existence several years before which had the mandate to increase, develop and facilitate economic development. Now it is doing away with that. It does not make sense. It does not make sense to the people in Saskatchewan. It does not make sense to the people in Quebec. It does not make sense to the people in Ontario nor the Canadians who happen to live on the island of Cape Breton.
I would have thought that since the senator in the other place is such an influential individual that the Minister of Finance would have seen his way and said: "We better go back and look at what has been said about this corporation and maintain it for its purposes are laudable. Its goals ought to be achievable and its results, if obtained, will have an immediate and positive impact on a society of our country", but that has not happened at all. In point of fact the Government of Canada is
doing away with it because it does not enjoy the support. I say so. You, Sir, being a distinguished and learned person of this Chamber might find my remarks to be somewhat cynical.
However, that agency is no longer in existence because it does not enjoy the support of the federal cabinet minister from Central Nova. It does not enjoy the support of the province of Nova Scotia, particularly the premier, Mr. Don Cameron. Those two individuals have been grossly, and I underline the word grossly, negligent. They have shown wanton disregard for those individuals living in that area of the country. By not standing up and fighting openly and publicly for the reinstatement of this agency, that for me, my constituents and the people living next door to me is a demonstrable sign that the compassion one expects from a national government just does not exist for those across the way.
I say that with great regret because there are good Tories. There are good Tories in my district. There are good Tories on the island of Cape Breton. I ask my good Tory friends: Do you agree with this measure to choke off this agency whose sole purpose was to create and enhance economic development? Do you now agree with the government of the day that it is no longer useful to maintain this particular operation?
I would have thought that the Minister of Agriculture would have stood in his place today and taken me to task for some of the comments I have made about him and his role in terms of the government cutbacks. However it falls now to the President of the Treasury Board to stand in his place and say that his colleagues have done the right thing, that the senator in the other place was either lying to the people of Canada, in particular to the people of Cape Breton, or as they say in my district and I say with great regret, that the senator in the other place was being careless with the truth.
We know that not only was he careless with the truth but he was also doing it for the sole political purpose in 1988 of trying to win seats in the province of Nova Scotia. Today they are capitulating to the provincial government of Don Cameron by doing away with Enterprise Cape Breton. The sole reason is that it is a political manoeuvre by the provincial premier and the hon. member from Central Nova. It is to punish those of us who have seen the wisdom as hundreds of thousands of Canadians have registered from coast to coast that the government
April 23, 1993

opposite is not just incompetent, it no longer deserves the support of the Canadian people.
We are being punished as a society. The President of the Treasury Board has a great knowledge of the distinct society and what it means for the province of Quebec. I hope he will tell those individuals in Cape Breton who also believe themselves to be a distinct society in many respects as to why they are being denied the opportunity to fully participate in the Canadian economy. I hope the minister will have the intestinal fortitude to stand in his place moments from now and defend this reckless and wanton disregard for a people whose region has an unemployment rate of 29.4 per cent.
Is it fair, Mr. Speaker? I know you, Sir. I have known you for a long time. You are distinguished and you are learned. You are responsible and fair. Is it fair? Is it fair to cut people adrift?
Now the minister will stand in his place and he will take out one of his pieces of paper and he will say: "This is what we have given those people down there. They are on Canada pension. They are on Canada pension disability. We have done this for Devco and we have done that".
We are not looking for handouts. We are looking for an opportunity to participate fully in the Canadian economy. We do not need any minister of the Crown doing the shameless things that have been done to the people of Cape Breton over the last number of years and more recently with the elimination of this particular development agency.
I say through you, Mr. Speaker, to all ministers opposite. I stand here today and I speak for those thousands of young people who are without work, whose only hope is to migrate out of that area to somewhere else. Then again the Canadian economy is so weak that there is nowhere else where the talents they have to offer can be accepted. I speak for the senior citizens down there who wish that their sons and daughters had an opportunity to make a meaningful life and to participate fully in the Canadian economy. I speak for the coal miners and all of those resource people in my constituency and other constituencies who wish to have meaningful work so that they can make a contribution to their

community, a contribution that many of us take for granted.
However, cutting this agency adrift will do absolutely nothing to enhance economic development. It will retard economic development on the island of Cape Breton.
I hope as this debate comes to an end the real reason will be given clearly in this Chamber. It is that we are being penalized in Cape Breton by the minister from Central Nova and the premier of the province, Don Cameron, because of the way in which we have voted in previous elections.
This was supposed to be the new wave, a different way of doing business, but it is the old practices of the Mulroney government at best, the Diefenbaker regime, and of course the Stanfield years in the province of Nova Scotia: Hit often but hit low; hit those that are least able to stand for themselves and hit those areas of the country that are least able to engender and to foster economic development.
That is what Bill C-93 does. It eliminates the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation. It eliminates those jobs and that purpose from government and from the national government. When I hear the hon. member from Ontario who stood in his place not moments ago and just made a passing reference, does he wonder why there is such antipathy? Does he wonder why there are such ill feelings toward other regions of the country, when we are treated like second class citizens? We do not want to be treated like second class citizens, because we are not second class citizens. It is high time that the government opposite took that into careful consideration when planning its mandate and election platform.
I fear that with this continual erosion of an economic base and the consistent and persistent battering of a community that there are very few alternatives left for that society to take. I make mention of civil disobedience, not to condone it, make no mistake about that.
However, I have seen far too many unemployed young people, far too many students who do not have sufficient income to pursue a post-secondary education, far too many senior citizens who do not have sufficient moneys to care for themselves and their families, far too many residents without the appropriate housing, far too many municipalities without the appropriate infrastructure. I

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleague for the question. He asked an important question.
My colleague should not be sucked into the ideology of the right which says in its essence, in its very form, that the only manner in which a deficit can be cut is to eliminate programs. Yes, there are programs. Yes, there are cuts that one could say, intellectually speaking that is, that we would agree with. However, where the Canadian economy is at the present time has to be one aspect of a much broader picture.
There is a crisis with the deficit but there is a crisis in unemployment. There is a crisis with interest rates in terms of the spread between Canada and the United States. The monetary policies of the government have not added anything. The mere fact is that the government has said its sole purpose was to fight inflation. You must have not only one goal, you must have several goals. It must be a balanced approach. Yes, there has to be deficit reduction, but it cannot be done in isolation
April 23, 1993

from other things. We cannot forget the unemployed, as my leader said quite aptly.
If you listen to the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of the Environment, Mr. Speaker, by getting rid of Veterans Affairs, old age security and medicare and have an unemployment rate of 25 per cent, you know what you have, you have a revolution on your hands. People are not going to put up with that. Therefore, it must be a balanced approach.
I say affirmatively to my colleague in answer to his first question that it must be part of a balanced program taking other matters such as unemployment, interest rates, property values, what have you, into consideration.

I realize there may not be one in Whitby but I suspect that if he looked and dug a little deeper he might find that some of these people live in his constituency. In any event, there are people from the University of Toronto, University of Ottawa, University of British Columbia, Universite de Montreal, Acadia University, Sir Wilfred Laurier University, University of Guelph, Carleton University, Dalhousie University, Universite Laval, University of Regina, University of Calgary and I could go on.
These people are appalled that this government would fail to listen to the voices of Canadians in the social science community of this country who feel their independence is being done away with and who see, in the short-sighted goal to save possibly $500,000 over five years and no more, that this government is selling them

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION (GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATIONS) ACT, 1992 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I particularly want to thank my colleague from Kingston and the Islands for his generous invitation to share with the House the very stimulating and passionate exchanges we have had about this bill over the past several months. I can say that I do represent that small but doughty group of people in the House of Commons who came from academic life, albeit a long time ago, and who find the purpose of this bill to be both nonsensical and particularly galling in terms of the objectives set out by the government.
Government Orders
It is interesting that we are debating this bill when a new budget is about to be presented on Monday. There is a very important lesson to be learned in this debate about how not to do budgets. I recall vividly the grand announcements made by the Minister of Finance about all the new mergers, integrations and combinations he was going to make in order to save taxpayers' money.
Bill C-93 was a direct product of that commitment, but lo and behold there is no money to be saved. This is a massive renovation that will substantially undermine the academic external university relations of this country and is to no purpose at all other than cosmetic reasons. It is simply action for its own sake. This is a government that has lost any connection between ends and means. It is unable to relate a piece of legislation to an objective. It is all done with the purpose of trying to create the illusion of action. The end result is to undermine, weaken and erode some very substantial institutions in this country.
I want to speak in particular to an aspect of the bill that has been brought to my attention and which I feel sorrowful about. That is the way in which the international academic relations program of the Department of External Affairs is being tom away from the international foreign policy agency of our country and merged into a new creation without any particular rationale given. Certainly nobody was talked to and nobody was asked for their opinion.
It comes at perhaps one of the most important turning points in the history of this country. We are beginning to realize the impact of globalization and are beginning to understand that the security, prosperity and well-being of this country is now very dependent upon our establishing a whole range of links throughout the world.
One of the most important connections we can make is in the area of academic exchange through having other countries understand more about Canada and having teachers and researchers working in their countries to ensure they understand the benefits of Canadian science, social sciences, humanities and culture. One of the most effective programs for undertaking that outreach on behalf of Canadians to the rest of the world has been the international academic relations program which has ensured a very constant and creative flow of people and ideas emanating from Canada around the world. It is part of our foreign policy. Foreign policy is no longer just a group of diplomats meeting in embassies to talk about

April 23, 1993
Government Orders
affairs of state. Foreign policy is now about the environment. It is about the movement of people. It is about the exchange of ideas. It is about developing new relationships between business and labour and universities and cultural organizations. One of the great and important impulses in the world ahead will be to broaden and enrich that diversity of connections and linkages.
At the time when an institution had been put in place, had been tempered by experience, was in a position to begin developing and expanding its role, what does the Conservative government do? It lops it off, turns it into a new agency, and the end result will be this. This new creation, whatever it is called, CHARC or CASH, I forget what the the acronym will be, is going to have to develop its own international outreach, its own officers, its own officials working in an international context which will compete with our own embassies abroad. We will now have a duplicate of function rather than an integrated function. We will be creating a competitive agency, having to go through all the pangs of start-up, getting new relations established, hiring people and beginning to reinvent the program all over again.
As a serious, rational thinker, Mr. Speaker, can you accept that as good public policy? Does that make sense in your eyes? It certainly does not make sense in the eyes of a wide range of institutions around the world. I have a file full of letters from different universities and research institutes around the world saying this is folly, this makes no sense, the government has gone cuckoo.
If people abroad can recognize that I guess the question is why cannot members of the caucus recognize it? I say to these members, if in the so-called time of constraint you had a legitimate case to make that actually large amounts of money were going to be saved, that it was going to be more efficient and more effective and more realistic and more rational, then all right. However every single piece of evidence, all testimony, every representation made by everybody who appeared before the committee or who have written letters, have said it simply is not going to work.
I put that on the table as an exhibit and a caution, that when we come to the next budget exercise and hear all the grand announcements on Monday, with the great
waves of applause emanating from the government benches about the new rationalization, remember Bill C-93. Remember what it does and does not do. It will not save money. It will create duplication, more bureaucracy, more competition at less cost and saving, and undermine a perfectly good program that has worked effectively on behalf of Canadians.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION (GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATIONS) ACT, 1992 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to my colleague outlining his reasons for not supporting Bill C-93. He feels, as I feel, there is not sufficient proof to show there would really be that much saving or that much efficiency. I agree with him. I have not seen any proof either.
There has been ample opportunity through the hearings in committee and through the letters we as members of Parliament have received. We have not received one letter showing that there would be substantial savings. If you do not have this kind of proof I do not see how you could support legislation, a bill that purports to make for efficient government administration or one that is supposed to save money.
I have heard that we are talking about $5 million, one and a half million dollars per year. Different amounts of money have been bandied about, and I am not sure really whether those numbers are verifiable or not, but there are some numbers that are verifiable.
In my comment I would just like to say the government will have the opportunity to show how it can streamline, how it can get lean, how it can cut into the deficit with the budget we are expecting some time next week.
There are certain things we could suggest here. One is not to pass Bill C-93 because it is certainly not the kind of approach we would like to see taken, but there are some things the government could do.
Being from Quebec, everyone knows the province of Quebec has been one of the most vociferous provinces in its demands that duplication of responsibilities, organizations and ministries be reduced as much as possible. In a spirit of non-partisanship and in the spirit of just looking logically at the situation, earlier I had asked one of my colleagues on the government side whether we could not look at perhaps fusing the Department of Finance and Revenue Canada.
April 23, 1993

I would also look at areas such as devolving to the provincial side the control of regional development. That would be very important. It would no longer be a slush fund where different ministers just before an election could create a Hibernia or all sorts of other programs which really do not have much bearing in reality or are not commercially sound.
I believe it is time for us to seriously look at cutting the expense of government but not necessarily the programs. We begin by sending a message to the electorate that we are serious about cutting certain government expenses that can easily be done away with. That is before going into the programs because then there would be no choice. If we do not move right away we will not have to trim programs but we will have to start eliminating them and I do not want to do that.
The question to my colleague is this.

speechtext: It is about time.

speechtext:

Does he see anything positive about Bill C-93? One of his colleagues said earlier in committee that he mentioned there were some positive aspects. Does he see anything positive at all or is it just entirely negative?

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION (GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATIONS) ACT, 1992 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I said in my remarks perhaps the most positive thing about the bill is its demonstration of how not to go about streamlining, rationalizing or making change. It has become more of an exercise in futility than an exercise in frugality and that has been part of the problem.
The necessary groundwork was not undertaken to develop an effective program on which we would give grants to culture, social sciences and international academic organizations. No one was consulted. No examination was done. No one was asked for their opinion. It was simply a fiat from the Department of Finance and the minister. I do not know the particular grudge it has against these organizations.
I think it was concocted more in the bowels of a public relations agency in trying to create the fantasy that something was being done to save the taxpayers money as opposed to a serious policy analysis. If there is any heuristic value in this motion-I find it hard both to say the word and attribute such a noble motive to the
Government Orders
government-it would be as a good way of how badly it governs.
